faqs.a: Tokens. Every price, limit and speed figure for a model is stated in tokens, so the rest of the vocabulary depends on it.
faqs.q: What should I learn first about AI?

faqs.a: Today the median API model tracked on this site costs $0.40 per million input tokens and $1.80 per million output tokens. Summarising a 40 page contract comes to about 1.2 cents at those prices.
faqs.q: How much does it cost to use an AI model?

faqs.a: Training builds a model from data and is done once, usually by the model's maker. Inference is every use of the model after that, and it is where most ongoing cost sits.
faqs.q: What is the difference between training and inference?

faqs.a: Use retrieval when the model needs your facts, because documents change and retrieval reads them at question time. Use fine-tuning when you need a different behaviour or style, not new facts.
faqs.q: Should I fine-tune a model or use retrieval?

faqs.a: A model produces the most likely continuation of text, not a checked fact. When the likely answer and the true answer differ, it states the likely one with the same confidence.
faqs.q: Why do AI models make things up?

name: Understand AI

steps.why: Everything a model reads and writes is counted in tokens, and so is everything it costs. Until this one is clear, no pricing page will make sense.

meet.fact: Today the median model tracked here costs $0.40 per million input tokens and $1.80 per million output tokens, across 447 models from 60 providers.
meet.name: API Pricing

terms.name: Token
terms.definition: The basic unit of text a model processes, corresponding to a word, part of a word, or punctuation. Billing, context limits, and speed are all denominated in tokens, roughly three-quarters of a word each in English.

steps.title: Start with the unit: the token

steps.why: The architecture underneath almost every current system, and the word for a large general model that others are built on.

meet.fact: The 1,000 most downloaded open language models on Hugging Face, refreshed daily.
meet.name: Large Language Models

meet.fact: 17 open source frameworks these models are built and trained with.
meet.name: AI Frameworks

terms.name: Transformer
terms.example: GPT, BERT, Gemini, and Claude are all transformers.
terms.definition: The deep learning architecture built on self-attention, introduced in 2017, that forms the foundation of modern LLMs. Its decisive property was parallelizable training, which let model scale grow with hardware in a way recurrent architectures never could.

terms.name: Foundation Model
terms.example: GPT, Claude, and Llama serving as bases for countless products.
terms.definition: A large model trained on broad data at scale that serves as the base for many downstream tasks. The economic point is amortization: one enormous training run, adapted cheaply a thousand ways.

steps.title: What the model is made of: transformer, foundation model

steps.why: How text becomes numbers a machine can compare. This is the idea that makes search, retrieval and recommendation work.

meet.fact: The 1,000 most downloaded open embedding models, the component that turns text into those numbers.
meet.name: Embedding Models

terms.name: Embedding
terms.example: Sentences mapped to vectors so related ideas sit near each other.
terms.definition: A vector representation of data in high-dimensional space where semantic similarity corresponds to geometric distance. The data structure that makes meaning computable, and the foundation under semantic search and RAG.

steps.title: How it represents meaning: embedding

steps.why: The working memory of a model, and the constraint behind most disappointing results. A model has not read your whole document unless the document fits.

meet.fact: The largest context window among the 447 API models tracked here is 2,000,000 tokens.
meet.name: API Pricing

terms.name: Context Window
terms.example: A 200 thousand token window holding an entire contract set for review.
terms.definition: The maximum number of tokens a model can process and retain during a single interaction: its working memory. Everything the model should consider, instructions, documents, history, must fit inside it.

steps.title: How much it can hold at once: context window

steps.why: Training builds the model. Inference is using it. Almost every cost a business actually pays is here, not in training.

meet.fact: 12 open source engines that run models efficiently on your own hardware.
meet.name: Inference Engines

meet.fact: 109 companies that run inference for you and bill per token.
meet.name: Model Serving Providers

terms.name: Inference
terms.example: A deployed model answering user prompts around the clock.
terms.definition: The live execution phase where a trained model processes inputs and produces outputs. Training happens once; inference happens forever, which is why inference economics dominate production cost.

steps.title: Running it: inference

steps.why: The two ways to change a model's behaviour without building one. Knowing which problem calls for which is most of the practical skill.

meet.fact: 8 curated datasets used to train and fine-tune models, with licence and gating.
meet.name: Training Datasets

terms.name: Fine-tuning
terms.example: A medical fine-tune adapting a general model to clinical language.
terms.definition: Taking a pre-trained model and continuing training on a smaller, domain-specific dataset to adapt it for particular tasks. The mid-price adaptation option: above prompting, below training from scratch, with governance duties attached, since tuned models inherit and can amplify data problems.

terms.name: Prompt Engineering
terms.example: Iterating a prompt against an eval suite until accuracy holds.
terms.definition: The practice of crafting, structuring, and optimizing inputs to elicit accurate and useful model output. Less mystical than its reputation: mostly clear specification, good examples, and systematic testing.

steps.title: Making it yours: fine-tuning, prompt engineering

steps.why: Feeding a model your own documents at the moment of the question, rather than retraining it. This is how most enterprise deployments actually work.

meet.fact: Retrieval runs on embeddings: your documents and the question are both turned into numbers, and the closest matches are handed to the model.
meet.name: Embedding Models

terms.name: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
terms.example: A document QA system answering from the company's own files, with sources.
terms.definition: An architecture that retrieves relevant context from external data sources before the model generates, so answers reflect current, private, or specialized information. The default enterprise pattern: it grounds answers, enables citations, and keeps knowledge updatable without retraining.

steps.title: Giving it your facts: retrieval

steps.why: A model that takes actions rather than only answering. Every governance and security question gets harder at this step.

meet.fact: 2,380 servers from the official Model Context Protocol registry, the standard way agents are given tools.
meet.name: MCP Server tracker

meet.fact: The open protocol for one agent to hand work to another, explained from its specification.
meet.name: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol

meet.fact: 4 open source agent projects tracked from their repositories.
meet.name: Autonomous Agents

terms.name: Agent
terms.example: A research agent that searches, reads, and compiles a briefing from one request.
terms.definition: An AI system that takes a goal, breaks it into steps, and carries those steps out using tools, rather than answering a single question and stopping. The defining trait is initiative between instructions: the agent decides what to do next.

steps.title: Letting it act: agent

steps.why: Confident output that is not true. Understanding why it happens, rather than treating it as a bug to patch, is the difference between a working deployment and a liability.

meet.fact: 9 curated benchmarks used to measure how often models get things right.
meet.name: Evaluation Datasets

terms.name: Hallucination
terms.example: An LLM citing court cases that do not exist, in perfect legal formatting.
terms.definition: A generative model confidently outputting false, fabricated, or unsupported information. The fluency is the danger: fabricated content arrives in the same authoritative voice as fact, which is why verification belongs in every AI workflow.

steps.title: Where it goes wrong: hallucination

title: Understand AI: a path through the glossary, in the order the ideas build
answer: The glossary on this site is alphabetical, which is right for looking a term up and wrong for learning the field. This page puts the terms in the order the ideas actually build on each other: what a model is made of, how it is trained, what it costs to run, how it is made useful, and where it goes wrong. Every step links to the full definition. Read top to bottom once and the rest of the site stops needing translation.

points.name: Why this order and not the alphabet
points.detail: A glossary answers a question you already know to ask. A path is for someone who does not yet know what to ask. The sequence here follows dependency: tokens before cost, context before disappointment, inference before budgeting, agents before governance.

points.name: Where to go next
points.detail: Once these nine are clear, three sections stop needing translation: the model catalogue, the compute and pricing pages, and the compliance material, because nearly every obligation in AI law is written about one of the steps above.

steps.text: A 40 page contract at about 500 words a page is roughly 20,000 words. At OpenAI's rule of thumb of about 0.75 words per token for English, that is about 26,700 tokens in, plus about 1,000 tokens for a one page summary out.
The model has to hold all 27,700 tokens at once. 430 of the 447 API models tracked here can, and 17 cannot, so for those the contract would have to be split.

At today's median prices, $0.40 per million in and $1.80 per million out, the read costs about $0.0107 and the summary about $0.0018, together about 1.2 cents. Price, not capability, is rarely the barrier at this size.
For a library of contracts rather than one, the whole library will not fit. Retrieval embeds every contract once and hands the model only the passages that match the question.
A summary can state a clause the contract does not contain. For anything with legal weight, the summary is a map to the pages to read, not a substitute for them.

example.title: One question through all nine steps: summarising a 40 page contract
example.assumption: Assumes about 500 words a page. Words per token is OpenAI's published rule of thumb for English text, and varies by language and model.

reading.body:
A 40-page contract costs about 1.2 cents to read and summarize at median API prices, and 421 of 438 tracked models can hold it in one context window.

At roughly 27,700 tokens total, the economics are trivial: $0.0107 to read and $0.0018 to summarize. For a single document, neither price nor working memory is the obstacle for most models, since only 17 of 438 cannot hold the full contract and would need it split.

The constraint appears when the task scales or when accuracy carries legal weight. A library of contracts will not fit in any context window, so retrieval embeds each document and hands the model only relevant passages. And a summary can state a clause the contract does not contain, so the output is a map to the pages to read, not a substitute for them.

What this does not cover is larger workloads, fine-tuning, or agentic action, and the median prices hide variation across the 60 providers. It also says nothing about the compute or power behind inference, only the per-token price a buyer sees.
